articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. A social media competitor analysis reveals how your brand compares to competitors across content, engagement, audience growth, and share of voice.
  2. The process follows five steps: identify competitors, define your metrics, gather performance data, run a SWOT analysis, and set up ongoing monitoring.

What is a social media competitor analysis?

A social media competitor analysis is the process of looking at your competitors’ social content and activity to understand how they compare to your own performance.

Done well, it does more than satisfy curiosity. It tells you where to spend your content budget, which formats to prioritize, and how quickly to respond when the market shifts.

When you run a competitor analysis, you can:

  • Spot who your real competitors are on social
  • See which platforms they’re active on
  • Learn how they use each channel (organic posts, paid ads, influencer partnerships, or a mix)
  • Spot new threats or emerging players
  • Identify gaps, quick wins, and opportunities in your own social presence

Why does social media competitor analysis matter in 2026?

Social media competitor analysis matters because it connects your social strategy to measurable business outcomes. Without competitive context, a 2% engagement rate is just a number. With it, you know whether you’re leading your category or falling behind.

A few things make this work more valuable right now. Content volume keeps climbing as 51% of content professionals now use AI to create posts, which makes differentiation harder and raises the bar for what stands out. Platform algorithms also reward relevance over frequency, so understanding which competitor posts actually land is more useful than counting how often they publish.

There’s a reporting angle too. Marketing leaders are regularly asked to justify social investment, especially with social advertising at 12.2% of budgets, and competitive benchmarking gives that case a credible reference point. It also shortens your reaction time: if a competitor shifts messaging, launches a product, or runs into a brand issue, you want to know before it becomes a trend.

Here’s what a solid competitive analysis on social media gives you:

  • Content gaps: Topics, formats, or audiences nobody in your category is serving well
  • Performance benchmarks: A realistic baseline for engagement, growth, and posting cadence
  • Early threat detection: New entrants, pricing moves, and messaging shifts
  • Budget justification: Competitive context that makes your resourcing case concrete
  • Positioning input: Evidence for how your brand should sound different, not just louder

Put simply, competitor analysis turns your social data from a scorecard into a decision-making tool.

What metrics should you track in a social media competitor analysis?

The most valuable metrics to track are the ones that show how competitors perform relative to your brand across content, audience, and engagement. You don’t need all of them. Pick the handful that map to your goals, then measure them consistently so trends mean something.

Engagement and growth metrics

Engagement rate is the clearest comparison metric because it normalizes for audience size. A competitor with 20,000 followers and strong engagement is often a better content benchmark than one with 500,000 followers and dead comment sections.

Follower growth rate adds the time dimension. Look at the trend over the last two or three quarters rather than a single snapshot, since campaigns and one-off viral posts can distort a month. Pair it with posting frequency to see whether more output is actually producing more growth, or just more noise.

Share of voice measures how much of the total conversation in your category mentions your brand versus competitors. It’s the metric that answers “are we part of the discussion?” rather than “did our post do well?”

articles.title: Google Adds Gemini 4 Argon To AI Mode For Pro & Ultra Subscribers via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Google has added Gemini 4 Argon to the AI Mode model menu for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The rollout comes on the same day the model became available to developers, enterprises, and Gemini app users.

Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, announced the rollout on X, saying Argon “is now rolling out globally in Search” and that subscribers can switch to it using the “+” icon.

Google’s first Argon announcement , 13 days ago, didn’t mention Pro subscribers. Today’s launch post lists them alongside Ultra subscribers, but nothing announced today changes the default for free-tier AI Mode users.

You can pick Argon from the “+” icon in AI Mode’s “Ask anything” bar, the same menu that added 3.7 Flash in August and 3.8 Flash in September.

Stein says Argon “brings big improvements to tackling nuanced, multi-step tasks in AI Mode” and is “better at understanding your intent and following your instructions in back and forth conversations.” The launch post makes a similar claim for the model as a whole, saying it “follows style instructions better than any of our previous Gemini models.”

Neither post states a language. The 3.7 Flash rollout was English only.

Since it’s rolling out, it may not be available to everyone just yet. As of 12:17 p.m. ET, Argon hadn’t appeared in the menu on my own Pro account.

Google introduced Argon on Sept. 30 as a frontier model for coding, enterprise knowledge work, and cyber defense, and released it to “a set of trusted cyber defenders” through its Fairwind Program . That post said the release to developers, enterprises, and consumers would come “as soon as possible” and would start “with paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers.”

Today’s post brings all the groups together at once. Developers can access it through the Gemini API’s paid tier, Ultra subscribers can use it in Google Antigravity, Google’s coding tool, and Pro and Ultra subscribers can find it in the Gemini app and AI Mode.

Gemini 3 Pro became available as an option in AI Mode in November. Since then, every addition to the menu I covered has been a Flash model. Gemini 3 Flash became the default in December, Gemini 3.5 Flash took over as the global default at I/O in May, Gemini 3.7 Flash joined the menu on Aug. 14, and 3.8 Flash followed on Sept. 2.

In February, I covered Google’s reasoning for running AI Mode on Flash models, which cost less and respond faster, so they can run at Search scale.

Google’s support page for AI Mode’s model menu, read today, still names only “Pro” and “Fast” as options and describes the Pro option as Gemini 3 Pro. It read the same way on Aug. 14 and Sept. 2.

Argon is available by subscription only, just like the two Flash models that joined the menu before it.

The improvements Google describes involve multi-step tasks and back-and-forth conversations, so a multi-step task with follow-up questions is the best way to test the claim. Once Argon appears in your menu, and if 3.8 Flash is still listed alongside it, try the same sequence with both models and note which one answers each time.

The next question is whether Argon will remain a subscriber option or become the default in AI Mode. Gemini 3 Flash and 3.5 Flash both launched as the default, while Gemini 3 Pro launched as an option and has remained one. Neither Google’s launch post nor Stein’s X post clarifies which direction Argon will take.

The launch post wraps up by saying it’s looking forward to “bringing you the rest of the Gemini 4 family,” but it doesn’t specify which of those models will be available in AI Mode.

articles.title: How much does YouTube pay per view in 2026?
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. YouTube pays per ad view, not per video view, typically an estimated $5 to $15 per 1,000 ad views in 2026.
  2. Your earnings per view depend on your content niche, audience location, ad type, video length, and seasonal advertiser demand.
  3. RPM (revenue per mille) shows what you actually earn after YouTube’s 45% cut, while CPM reflects what advertisers pay.
  4. Ad revenue is only one income stream. Brand deals, channel memberships, affiliate marketing, and merch can meaningfully increase total YouTube earnings.

How YouTube’s pay-per-view system works

YouTube does have a pay-per-view system, but it might not be what you’d initially think. Instead of getting paid for each video view, YouTubers are paid for each ad view.

Let’s dig a little deeper into what these two types of views mean:

  • Video views: The number of views your video gets.
  • Ad views: The number of views that ads on your video get.

YouTube pays you for the amount of ad views your video gets. If your video has a million views but no advertising on it, you won’t be making any money. If your video has a million views but only 10,000 ad views, you’ll be making money only on the 10,000 ad views.

Similarly, you might have multiple ads run within a single YouTube video. If users actually watch those ads all the way through, you could also end up with more ad views than video views.

Essentially, YouTube makes money off the advertising space, so it will only pay based on how much exposure your video generates for that advertising space. Of that advertising money, YouTube keeps 45% and you keep 55%. Through this model, YouTube has paid creators over $100 billion since 2021.

The short version: Your YouTube income is a share of ad revenue tied to ad views, not a flat rate per video view.

What are CPM, RPM, and CPC on YouTube?

CPM, RPM, and CPC are the three metrics that explain the gap between what advertisers spend and what lands in your bank account. They sound similar, but they measure very different things, and mixing them up is the fastest way to end up disappointed by your first payout.

Revenue per mille is the one worth watching. RPM is almost always lower than CPM because it accounts for YouTube’s 45% revenue share, plus all the views that never got an ad at all. A $12 CPM does not mean $12 in your pocket per 1,000 views.

So when you compare earnings numbers with other creators, check which metric they’re quoting. CPM tells you how valuable your audience is to advertisers, and RPM tells you what your channel actually earns.

How much does YouTube pay per 1,000 views in 2026?

In 2026, a YouTuber can earn an estimated $5 to $15 per 1,000 ad views. This is an industry estimate rather than a published YouTube rate, and because not every video view triggers an ad, your earnings per 1,000 video views land lower than that range.

According to Strike Social’s downloadable 2024 YouTube Ads Benchmark Report, YouTube ads see an average view rate of 49-68%, depending on factors like video ad type or creative. Using the middle of that range, here’s what estimated earnings look like at common view milestones.

Treat these as estimates, not promises. Your actual earnings shift with niche, audience location, ad formats, and the time of the year.

Can you make a full-time job out of being a YouTuber? Yes, but the math has to work at volume. A single 10,000-view video sitting in the middle of that estimated range brings in around $60. Publish one of those every day and you’re looking at roughly $21,900 a year, which isn’t a great salary on its own.

That assumes you stay stagnant, though. If you’re actually publishing new video content every day, or even once or twice a week, you should see compounding growth in views, subscribers, and ad revenue. And as you grow, you can layer in other monetization avenues.

How do you become eligible for ad revenue on YouTube?

You become eligible to earn ad revenue on YouTube by joining the YouTube Partner Program (YPP). The YPP is how you get YouTube money per view put into your pocket, and it has its own set of YouTube monetization requirements you’ll need to clear first.

articles.title: Brandweek 2026: The New Rules of Sports Partnerships ft. NWSL’s Jessica Goldstein
articles.fullContent:
By Jenny Rooney The old sponsorship model was simple: Buy the assets, activate around the big moment, and move on.

Jessica Goldstein thinks that model is already outdated.

Live from the Marketing Vanguard stage at Brandweek 2026, Jenny Rooney sits down with Jessica, VP of partnerships and marketing solutions at the National Women’s Soccer League, to unpack why modern sports partnerships need to behave more like platforms.

They also discuss the value of building campaigns on athlete storytelling, fan behavior, consistent presence, and a role the audience can actually recognize.

Why athlete storytelling can turn individual players into gateways to broader fandom

Why traditional sponsorship asset lists no longer create enough value on their own

How 360 partnership strategies can connect live moments, content and fan behavior

Why tentpoles need an always-on strategy around them to drive long-term value

Why data should inform partnership strategy without pretending to make every decision for you

How women’s sports can unlock categories and stories that traditional sports partnerships may not

This episode is part of a special vidcast series recorded live during Brandweek 2026 and presented in partnership with Tatari.

Jessica Goldstein is Vice President of Partnerships and Marketing Solutions at the NWSL, where she leads partnership strategy and marketing solutions for the league. Her work here primarily focuses on combining both sides of that experience: helping partners build stronger roles inside the league while using athlete storytelling, cultural crossover and long-term consistency to grow fandom around women’s soccer.

She has spent more than 20 years in sports, beginning at the NBA in production and entertainment before moving into brand marketing. Jessica  later spent more than 11 years agency-side, where much of her work focused on sponsorship strategy and building women’s sports platforms for major brands.

[03:19] Partnerships Can Actually Help Grow the Sport — Jessica  points to Google’s women’s sports strategy as an example of what happens when a partner brings more than media dollars. Google entered the WNBA before doing an NBA deal and focused on accessibility and discoverability. That included helping move games onto ESPN and ABC. The lesson: the strongest sports partnerships can create value for the brand while also making the sport easier for fans to find and follow.

[05:19] Athlete Storytelling Is a Growth Strategy — For Jessica , building the NWSL means building the athletes too. The more fans understand a player’s personality, interests and story, the more likely they are to follow that athlete, notice when they are playing and eventually tune into matches. The goal is not to expect every new fan to immediately watch every game. It is to create enough connection that following the athlete becomes an entry point into following the league.

[06:57] Sports Fandom Is Bigger Than the Game — Jessica  sees major opportunity in the crossover between sports, music, fashion, relationships and culture. Athletes show up at each other’s games. Fans follow what players wear, listen to and care about off the field. For the NWSL, that creates more storytelling territory than match results alone. Her point is that sports is culture, and brands that understand those intersections have far more ways to enter the conversation.

[09:03] The Asset-List Sponsorship Is Over — Jessica  argues that sponsorship cannot be reduced to a menu of rights and assets anymore. Brands need broader platforms and 360 strategies that connect live events, content, media and different fan behaviors. Not every fan watches every match, especially younger audiences. So the partnership has to meet them across different touchpoints. The value comes from creating a connected role around the fandom, not simply checking off contracted assets.

articles.title: Building a Brand Customers Believe In
articles.fullContent:
By Seth Simons This post was created in partnership with Fluent

Consumers can tell when a brand doesn’t have an authentic purpose—but they’ll go the distance for brands that do.

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ panel co-hosted with Fluent, Bill Bradley, deputy TV, media, and sports editor at ADWEEK, moderated a lively conversation focused on how brands turn purpose into performance.

Effective marketing creates a shared sense of purpose with the consumer, David Young, VP of retail media at DICK’S Sporting Goods, suggested, turning a transactional matter into an emotional one. “People need to recognize themselves in your message and what you stand for,” he said. At DICK’S, that means a belief that sports can change lives for athletes of every stripe.

Jeanniey Walden, CMO of Fluent, took this idea further, reasoning that brands should build experiences around their customers, then continue supporting and appreciating them beyond the point of sale. “The transaction is just the beginning of an entire journey that gives you purpose for what we’re all doing every day,” she observed.

So, how can brands prove that their purpose isn’t performative? For Perry Kamel, founder and CEO of DNA Vibe, it starts with ensuring a brand’s actions reflect its values. Earlier this year, DNA Vibe partnered with MoveUkraine to bring a production facility to Ukraine, where a local team assembles and distributes the company’s recovery devices to wounded veterans and civilians receiving care.

“How could we not do this?” Kamel asked. “Purpose is extremely powerful. It’s the first thing, but it’s got to be the real thing.”

Lois Cook, CEO of FootballHer and professional football player with the WFA, brings the same logic to her partnerships, ensuring that she only works with brands that share her own values.

“I have to be credible; there has to be integrity in what I do,” she stressed. “I can’t just join a company that doesn’t stand for anything, because who am I at that point?”

When consumers see a brand practicing what it preaches, Walden added, they trust it to meet their own needs. “When you create trust, you create belief in a brand,” she said. “When you create belief in a brand, that’s where the business grows.”

The panelists wrapped up by discussing challenges they’ve faced and the lessons they learned. For Robert “Gronk” Gronkowski, 4X Super Bowl champion, sports broadcaster, and entrepreneur, one lesson came early in his career: talent alone isn’t enough without the preparation to back it up.

“It doesn’t matter how talented you are in the NFL,” he shared. “If you don’t know the playbook, you’re not going to play.”

The lesson applies to marketers, too, who need a clear strategy to turn ideas and capabilities into results.

Walden shared an experience that offered a different perspective on what it takes to succeed, particularly when circumstances threaten the trust you’ve worked to build. At one of her first jobs, a cash-strapped startup, the CFO gambled away the media budget for a client who had followed her there out of trust. Instead of giving up, she took out a second mortgage on her house, paid for the media, and launched her own agency the next day with the client in tow.

“It’s really important that you show up, and when people put their trust in you, that you be there for them,” she concluded.

By Mark Mwachiro This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of September 28, 2026.

MS NOW finished the week as the only cable news network to record a gain in one of the measured demographics. The network had double-digit growth in the Adults 25-54 demo during total day, the lone bright spot across all measurements. The Versant network cemented its position as the No. 2 network in the demo during total day, at least this week.

On the other side, CNN was the only network to finish with losses across the board.

According to Nielsen big data + panel for the week of Sept. 28, Fox News averaged 1.631 million total viewers and 140,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network was down -2% in total viewers and -6% in the demo compared with the prior week ( the week beginning September 21 ).

During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.07 million total viewers and 94,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on its average from the previous week’s measurements, the network was flat in total viewers and down -4% in the demo.

Fox News remained in second place in total primetime viewership and slipped from No. 4 to No. 5 in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it remained first in total viewers and dropped from second to third in the total day demo.

MS NOW averaged 917,000 total viewers and 89,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network was down by -1% in total viewers and the demo compared with its primetime average the prior week.

During total day, MS NOW averaged 575,000 total viewers and 62,000 demo viewers. It was down -1% in total viewers but had a double-digit gain of +13% in the demo compared with the network’s average the prior week.

Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW remained third in total primetime viewers and was 15th in the demo. It also ranked third in total viewers and finished in eighth place in the total day demo.

CNN averaged 554,000 total primetime viewers and 97,000 demo viewers. It was down by -7% in total viewers and -1% in the demo compared to the previous week.

Among all cable networks, CNN dropped from fourth to seventh place in total viewers and was 11th in the demo during primetime, tied with HGTV. It remained at No. 4 in total day among total viewers and was No. 13 in the demo.

Key takeaways

  1. A “good” engagement rate falls between 1% and 5%, but what counts as strong varies significantly by industry and platform.
  2. Instagram leads overall engagement at 4.2% across industries, followed by LinkedIn at 3.9%.
  3. Construction, education, and nonprofits consistently post the highest average engagement rates across platforms.
  4. You can calculate your engagement rate with a simple formula, or use Perch by Hootsuite to track rates and benchmark against your industry automatically.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is the percentage of your audience that interacts with a piece of content, rather than just scrolling past it. It’s calculated by dividing total interactions by a measure of audience size (usually followers, reach, or impressions), then multiplying by 100.

What counts as an interaction depends on the platform, but it typically includes:

  • Likes: The lowest-effort signal of interest
  • Comments: A stronger signal, since they take real effort
  • Shares and reposts: Content worth passing along to someone else
  • Saves: Content people want to come back to
  • Clicks: Link clicks, profile visits, or taps on your content
  • DMs: Direct replies or message shares

The key thing to remember is that engagement rate measures quality of attention relative to audience size, which is why a small account can easily outperform a much larger one.

Why does engagement rate matter?

Engagement rate matters because it’s one of the few social media metrics that tells you whether your content actually connected with people. Follower counts and impressions measure exposure. Engagement measures response.

For marketing leaders, tracking the social media engagement rate across accounts serves four practical purposes:

  • Content quality signal: A dip in engagement often shows up before a dip in followers or conversions, making it an early warning system for content quality problems.
  • Algorithm input: Most platforms use engagement signals to decide how widely to distribute a post, so higher engagement compounds into more reach.
  • ROI indicator: Engagement rate normalizes for audience size, which makes it a fair way to compare performance across channels, regions, or business units.
  • Strategy guide: Comparing engagement by format and topic shows you what to produce more of, and what to stop making.

In short, engagement rate is the metric that tells you whether your audience cares, not just whether they saw it.

How do you calculate engagement rate?

You calculate engagement rate by dividing total engagements by an audience measure, then multiplying by 100. Which audience measure you use depends on what you’re trying to learn. There are three common methods:

  1. Engagement rate by reach, for judging content performance among people who saw it
  2. Engagement rate by followers, for benchmarking against industry averages
  3. Engagement rate by impressions, for paid campaigns and repeat exposure

Here’s how each one works. For more variations, including daily and cost-per-engagement formulas, see our full guide to measuring social engagement.

Engagement rate by reach

Formula: (Total engagements / Reach) x 100

This is the most accurate measure of content quality, because it only counts people who actually saw the post. Use it when you want to know how compelling a piece of content was.

Engagement rate by followers

Formula: (Total engagements / Followers) x 100

This is the most widely reported engagement rate formula, and the one used for the industry benchmarks below. Use it when you need to compare your performance to published averages.

Engagement rate by impressions

Formula: (Total engagements / Impressions) x 100

Impressions count every view, including repeat views, so this number runs lower than engagement by reach. Use it for paid campaigns where frequency matters. You can find additional formula breakdowns if you need to go deeper.

Note: If you’re calculating your account’s total engagement, include information about all your posts (e.g., total number of posts published, total number of likes, total number of impressions, and so on).

If you’re calculating the engagement rate of a specific social media marketing campaign, only include the details of the social media posts that were part of the campaign.

What is a good engagement rate?

A good engagement rate generally falls between 1% and 5%, depending on the platform and industry. Anything above 4% is strong on Instagram and LinkedIn, while 1.5% to 3% is closer to normal on TikTok and Facebook.

articles.title: Former TV Journalists Find Success Going the Independent Route
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro There is life after TV after all. Former ABC News correspondent Terry Moran ; former ABC News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jen Ashton ; and former ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News anchor Vinita Nair have taken their talents on the independent route.

Each journalist has recently launched their own independent outfit, joining many journalists who utilize digital publishing platforms to showcase their work, reach new audiences, and stay relevant.

Beehiiv has been the platform of choice for these veteran journalists. Launched in 2021, it has given journalists, creators, media companies, and brands the tools to publish, grow, and monetize their own audiences across newsletters, websites, podcasts, memberships, and other products.

Moran, who was let go from ABC News in June 2025, started Real Patriotism , combining his journalistic expertise in political reporting and analysis to provide content centered on current political discourse.

“It’s the best and hardest job I’ve ever had,” said Moran to TVNewser.

Ashton built her digital platform Ajenda , which focuses on nutrition, fitness, and wellness, from a one-person operation into a nearly 20-person business that generated seven figures in its first year and doubled revenue in its second. In addition, Ajenda has grown into two newsletters and a membership program, and it will soon launch a podcast and expand into live events.

“It’s been exciting and gratifying,” said Ashton on her new line of work.

Nair founded Vinita Speaks , a platform that coaches business leaders to communicate simply and confidently, and designs and facilitates customized communication training programs for global brands.

Her @vinitaspeaks TikTok account has more than 240,000 followers, and she also runs a newsletter.

“Building something I have complete control over has been the most fulfilling, educational, and unpredictable experience of my career,” said Nair.

As they embark on this new frontier, these three personalities shared additional thoughts with TVNewser about this new path and what it’s like to be an independent journalist.

Moran said everything he does, whether on air or in writing, comes from his own “reporting, analysis, and passion.” However, he acknowledged it can also be difficult because he is learning so much as an independent journalist, including production, business strategy, tech issues, and customer support.

Ashton said that for 18 years as a broadcast journalist, she never had a choice in topic selection. Since starting Ajenda, it has enabled her “to be more intentional and contemplative in the topics.”

Meanwhile, as an independent journalist, Nair recognized the unique opportunity in how communication was changing in real time. She made the pivot: “I was seeing how a digital, AI-centered world was affecting human connection, yet no one was reporting on it,” Nair said.

Though the job creates more independence, all three journalists noted they did miss the people they used to work with and offered high praise for their former teammates.

Still, independence creates autonomy and the ability to set your own schedule.

Ashton said she doesn’t miss the early wake-up calls and the heavy hair and makeup required for news networks, while Nair echoed similar sentiments, adding she doesn’t miss the long hours and unpredictable travel.

Moran said newsrooms can lack civic spirit, calling it “a rhetorical ornament, put up for show, rather than a democratic necessity and journalistic obligation.”

Establish credibility and build a connection

In this new space of journalism, being seen as a credible voice takes work, and as Nair pointed out, no newsroom staff validates your work; you have to do it all yourself.

“I use the same reporting standards and editorial judgment I developed in network news. Before I publish anything, I ask myself whether it is accurate, useful, and responsible,” Nair said.

However, credibility can take different forms with different audiences.

Moran says credibility is about getting it right and telling the truth about what it means, while Ashton says that in today’s world, having your name attached to a news organization doesn’t automatically make you a credible voice: “Being a good communicator with good credentials does,” Ashton added.

Don’t wait for the audience to come to you

Becoming an independent journalist isn’t easy, especially when you have to build and sustain audiences. Moran said that the main thing is to establish a connection with the audience, adding, “You’ll know you’re connecting by their authentic responses to the work.”

According to Ashton, a primary goal is establishing trust and authenticity with an audience. Nair added that her advice is to focus on your goals and make sure everything you produce follows that core idea.

For those considering this field, Ashton emphasizes patience and focus, noting that audiences won’t just come to you.

“You have to go to them. You need to find them, and they need to choose you as their source,” Ashton said.

Nair says you should be willing to take a risk within this new space, adding that you should use the skill sets that you have honed as a reporter to your advantage, using investigative experience to “understand what people need.”

Finally, Moran says your audience should get the truth from you: “Don’t fake outrage if you don’t feel it. Don’t run from a hard subject. Do follow your heart.”

articles.title: To Sell ChatGPT to Businesses, OpenAI Is Going Back to Field Marketing
articles.fullContent:
By Trishla Ostwal OpenAI may be one of the world’s most recognizable AI brands. To sell its business, its strongest marketing channel is decidedly offline.

“Field is the one I would definitely put out as our strongest channel right now,” said Leila Woodington, OpenAI’s head of B2B marketing, EMEA, during a panel at Semrush Spotlight in London today.

The reason is the gap between using ChatGPT and buying it. Most people know the product, Woodington said, but that awareness does not tell a company how to deploy it across thousands of employees, or persuade several executives who sign off on the purchase.

In-person events are one piece of a broader effort by the ChatGPT maker to explain the product to businesses. OpenAI also works with what Woodington called a “bench of really carefully curated creators and influencers who genuinely love our products,” who are brought in when the company ships something new, alongside leveraging social media.

OpenAI doubled its sponsored Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT from 61 in June to 122 in July, according to Business Insider .

“This is a complex buying decision that we’re influencing,” said Woodington. “No single one of those things is going to persuade the CEO of Fortune 500 companies to buy our technology.”

OpenAI Wants ChatGPT Ads to Become a Permanent Line Item in Agency Media Plans But keeping a constant brand message is its own challenge as OpenAI’s product lineup grows.

The company launched Dots , a persistent AI agent, at its developer conference in San Francisco last month alongside a plethora of tools. Instead of building a fresh campaign for each launch, Woodington’s team runs a fixed calendar, including about two webinars a month, and slots new products into it.

“We have a set of activities that are predefined, and then we plug launches into them, rather than taking every single launch and then spinning our wheels trying to figure out a way to get it to market,” she said.

The company is also building local teams in the markets it sells to, including people who understand local languages, cultures, and trade organizations.

Woodington, who previously spent more than a decade building Facebook’s B2B marketing function before working at Snap and an AI-powered video startup, joined OpenAI more than a year ago to help build its marketing operation.

“[CMOs] seem to expect that I’m completely on top of every single AI technology, at least within our own tools,” Woodington said. “[But] we are trying to keep up in the same way as others.”

articles.title: Google Says Why Site Migrations Can Exceed 4 Months via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Google’s John Mueller suggested that a change of address for a domain and website can take longer than four months to process. He also provided insight on how to prevent that from happening in order to have a better outcome.

A site owner reported on Reddit that they had a successful domain migration at the beginning of 2026 and everything progressed relatively smoothly with traffic fully recovered by April.

Four months later Google restored the old domain’s search visibility, essentially deindexing the new domain and resurrecting the old version in the search results. Site visitors clicking to the old domain were still being redirected to the new version, which search console began reporting as crawled but not indexed.

“So I have a website that was doing very well, especially on Google. At the start of 2026, I changed the name and domain so that one additional topic could be covered. Did all the redirects, Change of Address, and internal name changes right away so traffic recovered quickly around the start of April.

Everything was indexed on the new site and the new domain was getting around 5,000 impressions per day. Four months later, Google suddenly reverted everything back to the old domain.

More than 5,000 pages of the new domain were changed to Crawled, Not Currently Index and the new domain now gets 20 impressions per week.

But if I open GSC on the old domain, everything is there. The entire old domain was suddenly indexed all over again and all the impressions and clicks are showing there.

So one post shows up on Google under the old domain and when you click it, it redirects to the same post under the new domain and counts as a regular view for the new domain.

Why would Google suddenly revert this four months after everything was fixed? How do I fix this? Do I actually have to fix this since the impressions and clicks are still there, just being redirected?”

The person sharing their experience doesn’t say if they crawled their new domain to see if there are any internal links that are hardcoded with absolute URLs using the old domain name instead of using a relative URL.

Absolute URL: www.example.com/some-page.html

Sometimes absolute URLs can sneak into the site navigation, footer navigation, or within the content itself as contextual links. The best way to catch those is to give the old domain a full crawl with Screaming Frog prior to the domain name migration in order to identify those stray absolute internal links.

Another critical detail missing is how they redirected the old domain to the new domain. Was it a domain registrar-level redirect that preserves URL paths or was it a URL to URL redirect? The registrar-level redirect might not preserve file paths. HTTPS forwarding may fail if the old domain doesn’t have an SSL certificate.

Another issue that can potentially complicate a migration are chained redirects.

And here’s a big one: Redirects can sometimes fail when or if the navigational structure on the new site changes.

Lastly, the person asking the question on Reddit did not indicate if they updated their XML sitemap. This matters because XML sitemaps communicate preferred canonical URLs to Google. If the sitemap still lists the old domain, it could send conflicting canonicalization signals during the migration.

Google explicitly mentions the usefulness of sitemaps as part of a URL migration:

“Submitting a sitemap can help make the discovery process quicker, and it’s fine to move your site in sections.”

That advice presumes that the sitemap is for the correct domain name, right?

Google’s John Mueller offers his inside knowledge of other things to avoid.

John Mueller’s Advice For A Successful Domain Migration

Mueller responded that sometimes the domain name migration can take an extra long time. He also recommended doing a search console change of address for both WWW and non-WWW versions of the domain name.

“Happy to take a look if you want to DM me the domains. Sometimes things just take a particularly long time to be fully processed.

One thing which we noticed (and adjusted in the documentation a while back) that can help is to make sure that you have change of address set up in search console for both www and non-www , so that it can fully migrate the domain.”

The WWW and non-WWW domain versions of URLs for a change of address is a good catch. There could be links from outside of the site that are linking to one or the other that could be contributing to Google choosing the old domain as the canonical.

For diagnosing a site migration gone wrong, it’s not unreasonable to approach it as a canonicalization issue. Canonicalization is when Google chooses one domain or URL over all others as the one to index and rank.

articles.title: Personal branding: What it is and how to build yours
articles.fullContent:
You’ve heard it from mentors, recruiters and that coworker who posts on LinkedIn every morning: You need a personal brand. Truth is, you already have one, because people form a public perception of your brand whether you shape it or not. This guide shows you how to take control of that perception and turn it into real opportunities.

Personal branding once sounded like a celebrity-only game. Today, founders, marketers, job seekers and employees use it to stand out in crowded feeds and earn trust before they ever say hello. It’s how people decide whether to follow you, hire you or buy from you.

Branding yourself feels daunting when you don’t know where to start. But the strongest personal brands are built on who you already are.

You don’t need a massive following, a big budget or a magnetic personality. You need well-defined goals, a sharp sense of your value and the habit of showing up.

Ready to build yours? Let’s dig in.

What is personal branding?

Personal branding is how you present yourself as an individual to your audience. It’s the mix of expertise, values and personality people associate with your name. Our glossary definition covers the short version, and this guide shows you how to build one.

The idea isn’t new. Management writer Tom Peters popularized it in 1997 with his Fast Company essay “The Brand Called You.” Social media turned his idea into something anyone with a phone can act on.

Think about how corporate branding works. We associate specific feelings, values and expectations with brands we trust. Every company has a story and image.

The same applies to you and your personal brand. The difference comes down to who owns it, how it sounds and what it’s for.

People often treat personal branding as a synonym for being an influencer. It doesn’t have to be. A software engineer, a nurse and a small business owner can each build a personal brand without chasing fame.

Your brand should highlight your human side. Voices and personalities set brands (and people!) apart. Branding yourself means aligning your online persona with your real-life one.

Building your brand goes beyond just marketing yourself. Here are the key pieces of a personal brand:

  • Voice and values. That is, what you say and what you believe. Your brand voice shouldn’t be one-size-fits-all or robotic.

  • Content. What you create, and how you present it, attracts your audience. If you write long-form newsletters, mastering Substack SEO gets those deep dives discovered by new readers.

  • Creativity. You don’t need to be a creative genius to build a personal brand. But some sort of creative trademark helps you stand out from the crowd.

  • Personality. There’s no one-size-fits-all personality type for your brand. Energetic, laid back or suit-and-tie, you do you.

  • Authenticity. Your personal brand shouldn’t feel manufactured or made up. Align your online persona with who you are offline and your brand will never feel forced.

Why is personal branding important?

Here is why building a personal brand is worth the effort.

Standing out from the crowd

The people who’d benefit the most from a personal brand are often focused on building something else. A company, art, you name it.

Like it or not, everyone’s a content creator now. That means who we are and what we make are often one and the same.

Among the countless creators and marketers out there, growth is daunting. Your audience only has so much attention to give.

With a compelling brand and consistent content, you give yourself a chance to shine. People don’t grow audiences or garner influence by accident. And both your personal brand and what you create sit within your control.

Relatability and authenticity matter to modern audiences

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, consumers rank authenticity and relatability as two of the three most important brand content traits. Apply the same logic to individuals. This matters even more in an era where “influence” can feel manufactured.

That’s your edge as an individual. Nobody else has your experiences, your opinions or your sense of humor.

Making stronger connections with your community

Your voice and values shape your ability to grow your audience. Putting your personality front and center attracts like-minded followers.

That also means engaging with your audience to understand their needs and challenges. This goes hand in hand with establishing trust and building meaningful relationships.

When followers feel seen, they comment, share and come back for more. That’s how an audience becomes a community.

Opening doors to career and business opportunities

A strong personal brand puts your expertise on display before anyone asks for it. Recruiters, clients, collaborators and event organizers find you, instead of the other way around.

The 2025 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report found that thought leadership builds trust and opens doors where ads and traditional sales methods fall short. When you share your expertise in your own voice, you become the kind of thought leader buyers want to hear from.

What makes a strong personal brand?

A strong personal brand is specific, consistent and rooted in real value. Before you post anything, get well-defined answers to these questions.

  • Purpose: Why you’re building a brand at all (a new role, clients, a community or a product launch).

  • Niche: The narrow topic you want to be known for. Precision is memorable and breadth is forgettable.

  • Audience: The specific people you want to reach and the problems they need solved.

  • Value: What you give that audience that no one else does (expertise, perspective, entertainment or community).

  • Story: The experiences that explain why you care and why people should listen to you.

Pull those answers into a short personal brand statement. For example: “I help early-stage founders turn customer conversations into content that sells.”

Use that statement as a filter. If a post, bio or partnership doesn’t support it, skip it.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AnswerThePublic now functions as a content creation platform. It reads your URL, builds a Business Summary, and turns real audience questions into 50 ranked content ideas.
  • Suggested For You tells you what to write next, and Keyword Coverage tags every keyword you already rank for by source (sitemap, competitor, manual/planned, or AI suggestion) so you know where you stand today.
  • Content Studio drafts a full article in your brand voice, and one click publishes it straight to WordPress or shares it across your connected social accounts.
  • Ubersuggest’s AI Prompt Ideas tool surfaces the prompts people run for your keyword, which brands get mentioned, and which sources get cited inside those AI answers.
  • Ubersuggest’s AI Search Visibility report tracks how often your brand shows up in AI-generated answers over time, compares that to competitors, and flags whether the mentions read positive, neutral, or negative.

Search listening still gets you ahead in the SEO game. It just means something bigger now.

Hear me out.

Google averages 3.5 billion searches a day. About 20% of those have never been typed before.

Every search is a window into what someone actually thinks, wants, or worries about. And now, that window matters more than ever, since a huge share of those searches never end in a click. They end in an AI-generated answer. So, if your content isn’t built to be cited inside that answer, it doesn’t matter how good it is.

Google’s exactly where people still go when someone tells them to “just Google it.” But increasingly, they’re also asking ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Gemini the same questions.

By listening to what people are actually asking, across all of it, AnswerThePublic turns real search behavior into a content plan. Not a keyword list. A plan.

Pair it with Ubersuggest, and you’ve got the two halves of a real SEO strategy: what to write, and whether it’s working.

What is AnswerThePublic?

AnswerThePublic used to be a keyword ideation tool. Type in a word, get a wheel of related questions.

It’s grown into something bigger: a content intelligence and creation platform. You still start from real audience questions, but now the tool takes you all the way from “what should I write?” to a published article, in one place.

Say you run an ecommerce store selling earbuds and headphones. You could guess what your customers want to know. Or you could paste your site’s URL into AnswerThePublic and let it tell you, based on what real people are actually searching.

How to Use AnswerThePublic: An Example

Let’s head to AnswerThePublic.

Step 1: Enter your URL.

Instead of starting with a keyword, you start with your website. AnswerThePublic reads your site and builds a Business Summary in seconds: what you sell, who you sell to, and the topics you should own.

If you’d rather start with a specific topic, you can do that too. But the URL-first approach means the tool already knows your business before it gives you a single idea.

Step 2: Open Suggested For You.

In the past, this is where the wheel lived, full stop. Now you get the wheel plus something new: 50 AI-suggested content ideas, ranked by opportunity for your specific business, with a badge showing how likely that keyword is to rank well based on competition and content gaps.

articles.title: 8 best link-in-bio tools for brands and creators in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Between character count limitations and linking restrictions, one clickable URL in your bio could fix a lot of problems.

Link-in-bio tools let you centralize your social links with a dynamic landing page that hosts all the URLs for your social posts. That means a single link will lead to many destinations. You just need to update the landing page with the destination URL for every new post you share on your socials.

Your bio link stays the same, but people still get to visit the intended destination for your latest posts.

So link-in-bio tools for Instagram are especially useful for bypassing the platform’s restrictions against clickable links in the caption. This leads to real traffic that you could otherwise lose without a clickable URL to lead visitors to the right destination. And traffic could ultimately turn into conversions.

In this post, we rank the best link-in-bio tools to back up your social media efforts. Let’s dive in.

1. Sprout Social

Best for: Social teams that need link-in-bio features baked into a larger social media workflow

SproutLink is a built-in link-in-bio tool that comes with your Sprout Social plan. It lets you build a custom landing page featuring a clickable, shoppable grid that mirrors your Instagram. So when people click on your bio link, it’s easier to pick up where they left off on the platform.

You can create a custom branded URL that adds credibility to your link, giving audiences the confidence to click through. Sprout’s analysis even found that our link-in-bio Instagram tool led to a 17% average lift in profile engagement per day for customers using SproutLink.

The feature integrates with the rest of your Instagram publishing workflow, which means you get to add the destination links as you create and schedule new posts. And the clickable posts will automatically appear in your custom landing page.

This saves you the trouble of using a dedicated tool to add and manage your links separately from your publishing ecosystem.

Key features:

  • Custom branded URL
  • Visual grid-style landing page
  • Hourly-updated link analytics
  • Link scheduling
  • Branding and customization

Pros:

  • Seamless integration with social media management workflows
  • Robust analytics insights into page views and per-post click counts

Source: Sprout Social

2. Linktree

Best for: Solopreneurs and individual creators needing a tool with fast, no-frills setup

Linktree is a straightforward tool often touted as the “original” in the link-in-bio category. You can choose from pre-built designs to create a landing page that hosts all your links in one place.

The tool connects your content across different social networks, not just Instagram. You can even use QR codes to send offline traffic to your Linktree page.

The free tier lets you manage an unlimited number of basic links and comes with limited analytics. Upgrading to a paid plan unlocks deeper analytics and customization tools.

Key features:

  • Multi-platform link management
  • Supports unlimited links
  • QR codes for offline traffic
  • Traffic monetization support
  • Basic publishing and scheduling tools

Pros:

  • Free tier available
  • Easy, beginner-friendly setup

Cons:

  • Branding and customization require paid upgrades
  • Bare-bones analytics with the free plan

Source: Linktree

3. Beacons

Best for: Creators needing a tool to monetize their social media links

Beacons is an all-in-one creator platform with a built-in link-in-bio tool. It functions as a creator-commerce suite rather than a simple link page. So in addition to managing your URLs, you get to build a unified business hub featuring images, music, products and signup forms.

The free plan comes with basic analytics and a customizable link in bio. Custom domains and advanced marketing features require a paid upgrade.

Key features:

  • Built-in storefront
  • Multimedia embedding
  • Email capture, media kits, tipping
  • Digital products and affiliate links
  • Auto-updating media kits
  • Basic link analytics

Pros:

  • Free tier available
  • Robust monetization features

Cons:

  • Functions separately from your publishing workflow
  • 9% seller fees with the free plan

Source: Beacons

4. Milkshake

Best for: Beginners needing a fast, visual, mobile-first builder

Milkshake positions itself as a “website builder” rather than a link-in-bio tool. You can build a custom website by putting together multiple “Cards” (or pages) that each serves a specific purpose. articles.title: How Atlas Copco Group built a proactive reputation intelligence model
articles.fullContent:
Reputation risk often shows up in small ways first. Customer concerns in one market, inconsistent messaging in another. Different teams respond to the same issue in different ways. Individually, they may seem minor. Together, they can reveal a much bigger problem.

Part of the challenge is how brands track reputation risk in the first place. Traditional approaches often focus on obvious changes after they happen, rather than connecting social and media signals that could point to an issue sooner. As a result, teams can miss early warning signs or struggle to piece them together quickly enough.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that most teams take one to two weeks to act on what they see on social, while only 10% respond within hours. This delay has real consequences. Eighty-six percent of organizations say siloed or slow-moving insights have caused them to miss opportunities, and 26% have seen customer issues escalate that could have been addressed earlier.

Atlas Copco Group, a global industrial company spanning air compression, vacuum, industrial and power technologies, wanted better visibility into those warning signs. Their approach shows what it looks like to move beyond monitoring and use reputation data more proactively. This article breaks down their process to show what a stronger reputation intelligence model looks like in practice.

What is reputation intelligence? (And why monitoring no longer cuts it)

Reputation intelligence connects brand data across markets, channels and social accounts so teams can spot patterns, understand them and decide what needs attention.

Reputation monitoring, on the other hand, focuses on tracking what’s already happening around your brand. It tracks signals like reviews, mentions and shifts in sentiment. Monitoring helps teams keep tabs on public perception, while reputation intelligence adds the context needed to make more proactive decisions.

For large organizations, that broader view turns scattered brand feedback into clearer guidance for communications, go-to-market strategies, governance and other business decisions. Teams can use the same reputation data to identify recurring issues and give leaders a better view of developing risks in the business.

Reputation risk hides in small signals, not big spikes

Many reputation management services focus on obvious changes, like a sudden spike in negative sentiment or a surge in brand mentions. By then, the issue is already visible enough to demand a response or have caused damage.

The first clues are usually less obvious. Maybe your customers start complaining about the same thing or more of their questions go unanswered. Engagement might drop or online conversations about your brand might take on a more negative tone.

When Atlas Copco Group’s team dug into how conversations about their brand actually evolved, they saw that many risks started as smaller patterns: repeated questions, inconsistent account activity, off-brand content, inactive pages, declining quality signals or fragmented local execution.

These signals are easy to miss when you rely on alerts alone because each one can seem too minor to warrant attention. With social intelligence, Atlas Copco Group brings those signals together to spot patterns that need a closer look before they impact business performance.

Atlas Copco Group’s 5-step reputation intelligence model

Atlas Copco Group manages social in multiple business areas, divisions and local markets. Operating at this scale means protecting brand trust and compliance while enabling local teams to respond quickly to their audiences.

The team addressed that challenge by shifting from reactive reputation management to a more proactive governance model, earning Atlas Copco Group Sprout’s 2026 Predictive Edge Award.

The model is based on five practices that help them spot emerging risk, strengthen brand presence and manage issues consistently.

1. Catch weak signals early

Atlas Copco Group tracks weak signals that could point to larger reputation issues. Recurring customer and internal team behavior patterns are all indicators that brand consistency or account health may be slipping. Tracking these patterns across markets helps the global team focus on the bigger picture and provide guidance so local teams can stay close to their audiences and market.

To identify which weak signals matter for your brand, start with the reputation risks you already monitor and work backward. What behaviors, questions or changes tend to show up before those risks become more serious? Those early indicators can become the signals your team tracks more closely.

Using Sprout Social Listening, the Atlas team tracks these patterns across channels and spots connections that might be easy to miss when looking at each account on its own. From there, the team can then investigate what’s happening and decide whether a local market needs more guidance.

2. Establish a clear governance framework

Early signals are more useful when teams know what to do with them. Atlas Copco Group created a social media action matrix that sets clear expectations around account ownership, daily content checks and account health scorecards published every six months.

Those shared expectations also strengthen brand safety. When multiple teams and contributors manage social accounts, clear ownership and review processes create more consistency around how teams publish content and respond to potential issues.

Atlas Copco Group uses Tagging in Sprout to organize content by quality and compliance, track which teams are meeting brand standards and identify where additional support is needed.

3. Standardize account health metrics

Atlas Copco Group uses a consistent set of metrics to evaluate brand health in various markets. The team looks at activity, brand compliance, response times and audience engagement together to create a more objective view of performance.

You spend years managing a vibrant, positive brand reputation—nailing the customer experience, delivering great service and watching your reputation thrive. But all it takes is one viral post to make that hard work feel like it’s disappearing overnight.

Even the most experienced marketers face this reality. According to an Axios Harris Poll, 46% of corporate reputations have declined between 2019 and 2025.

Managing brand sentiment can feel overwhelming, but you can take control of your brand’s narrative with a smart corporate reputation management strategy.

What is corporate reputation management?

Corporate reputation management is the practice of proactively influencing and maintaining how the public perceives your brand. This includes monitoring conversations about your company, resolving issues quickly and amplifying positive moments to shape your brand perception.

Corporate reputation management and online reputation management go hand-in-hand. And when a crisis happens, 64% of consumers say it’s important for a brand to respond publicly on social media rather than through a press release or website statement. This is why social media teams are on the front lines, tasked with protecting and nurturing brand reputation.

A great example of managing a ‘crisis’ online—and getting ahead of the conversation— is the 2018 #ChickenCrises. When KFC ran out of chicken and had to shut down over 750 stores, customers were not happy. Using social listening, the brand noticed the backlash brewing online and quickly addressed the issue with an edgy, self-aware response. They rearranged the letters “KFC” on a chicken bucket to look like a curse word, essentially saying: “We messed up.”

This light-hearted, authentic response defused tension, protected the brand’s reputation and sparked viral trends. And there’s a reason we’re still talking about it eight years later: it’s become an iconic example of a brand apology. It reinforces how vital it is for social media professionals to listen, engage and collaborate with stakeholders to manage reputation challenges to shape brand perception.

As a marketing leader, your opportunity is to proactively build and protect corporate reputation by engaging with audience conversations and influencing your company’s narrative, wherever it happens.

Your reputation shapes every part of your business, from winning stakeholder trust to driving sales and building customer loyalty. Because reputation is foundational to brand health, damage to it is one of the biggest risks companies face today.

In highly regulated sectors like financial services, social media acts as an early warning system; a single misunderstood fee structure or service outage can escalate into a compliance nightmare if not addressed with immediate, transparent communication.

The classic Harvard Business Review’s Reputation and Its Risks, notes that 70-80% of the modern economy’s market value comes from “hard-to-assess intangible assets,” like brand equity. What is data storytelling?

Data storytelling is the practice of using facts, statistics, and quantitative information to build a compelling narrative that an audience can understand and act on. In other words, it uses real numbers to support an engaging story and authenticate the story’s message.

“Using data to tell stories from a brand’s point of view can be very effective, as it bridges that place between logic and emotion and lets a brand connect with a reader on a deeper level,” says Leeann Froese, Digital Marketing Manager at Town Hall Brands.

That brings us to another important part of data storytelling: the numbers need to be true, unaltered, and preferably provided by a trusted third party. Making up numbers or bending statistics to suit your own needs is a dangerous game, especially on social media.

Every good data story rests on three things working together: the data itself, the narrative around it, and the visuals that carry it.

What are the three pillars of data storytelling?

The three pillars of data storytelling are data, narrative, and visualization. Drop any one of them and the story falls flat: data alone is dry, narrative alone is unproven, and visuals alone are decoration.

Data

The foundation is accurate, relevant, and verifiable information. That might be third-party research, platform data, or your own first-party numbers from sales, surveys, or social analytics.

Whatever the origin, it needs to come from trusted sources you can name publicly. If you cannot point to where a number came from, it does not belong in the story.

Narrative

Narrative is what gives the numbers meaning. It supplies the context (why this matters now), the stakes (who is affected), and the takeaway (what the audience should do next).

A 12% increase is just arithmetic until you explain what changed and who it changed things for. That framing is what moves a stat from forgettable to shareable.

Visuals make data accessible and memorable in a feed built for speed. “The brain processes visual information much faster than text,” says Froese.

The format should match the message. Single-stat graphics work for one big number, bar charts for comparisons, line charts for change over time, and carousels when the story needs a few beats to land.

The 5 C’s of storytelling are Context, Characters, Conflict, Climax, and Closure. It is a classic narrative arc, and it maps neatly onto data storytelling when you treat your audience as the characters and your insight as the climax.

Used together, the 5 C’s keep a data post from becoming a list of figures. They give the numbers a beginning, a middle, and a reason to care.

articles.title: How to build brand loyalty: 7 strategies that work for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Brand loyalty is the emotional connection that drives customers to repeatedly choose one brand over alternatives, even when cheaper or more convenient options exist.
  2. Loyal customers cost less to retain than new ones cost to acquire, spend more over time, and actively recommend the brand to others.
  3. Building brand loyalty in 2026 requires consistent experiences, personalized engagement, fast customer care, and smart use of AI to anticipate customer needs.
  4. Key metrics for tracking brand loyalty include net promoter score, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, and sentiment analysis.

What is brand loyalty?

Brand loyalty is the connection between a brand and a customer that drives someone to make repeat purchases from a specific brand. They stick with that brand even when alternative suppliers or products may be cheaper or more easily accessible.

The lineup outside the Apple Store to get the latest iPhone the first morning it’s available? That’s brand loyalty in action.

What separates loyalty from habit is the emotional connection behind the purchase. A habitual buyer picks your product because it’s there. A loyal customer picks it because it says something about who they are, and because they trust you to deliver. That trust is built over time through familiarity with your brand (also known as brand awareness), satisfying early experiences, and consistency after the sale.

[contentuprade]

Brand loyalty vs. customer loyalty

Brand loyalty and customer loyalty sound interchangeable, but they come from different places. Brand loyalty is emotional and identity-driven. Customer loyalty is usually transactional, powered by price, points, or convenience. Both are worth having, but only one survives a competitor’s discount.

The brand loyalty pyramid

The brand loyalty pyramid was developed in the 1990s by David Aaker, hailed as “the father of modern branding.”

Just as the sales funnel shows how potential buyers move through the conversion process, the brand loyalty pyramid shows how customers move through the process to becoming brand-loyal.

The pyramid has five stages:

  • Switchers: People who have bought your product but are just as likely to buy a competitor’s product next time.
  • Habitual buyers: People who buy your products out of habit but could easily be swayed to another product if it’s cheaper or more convenient.
  • Satisfied buyers with switching costs: People who are satisfied with your brand but primarily stick with your products because there are barriers to switching (such as learning how to use a new tool or platform, or having to buy new cords or accessories).
  • Buyers who like the brand: At this point the connection becomes emotional, and the buyer becomes passionate about your brand for reasons they may not be able to articulate clearly.
  • Committed buyers: These are the people lining up to buy a new product the moment it launches. They love your brand and aren’t afraid to show it.

Source: Aaker, D.A. (1991) Managing Brand Equity. The Free Press, New York.

Why is brand loyalty important?

Brand loyalty matters because it lowers what you spend to grow and raises what each customer is worth. It’s obvious that you want people to choose your brand over your competitors. Brand loyalty ensures they do so again and again. But it provides more value to your brand than the simple revenue from customer retention and each purchase. Here’s why.

How loyal customers reduce acquisition costs and increase lifetime value

Acquiring a new customer is harder (and more expensive) than selling to a repeat customer.

Part of that is targeting efficiency. The more interaction you have with a customer or prospect, the better you can personalize your offers. Plus, you can target specific conversion goals (upsell? refill?) rather than using CPM awareness marketing campaigns.

Loyalty also cushions you when budgets tighten. When consumers cut back, the brands they already trust are the ones they keep buying, which makes retained revenue more predictable than new-customer revenue during uncertain periods.

Brand loyalty increases your lifetime customer value. That, in turn, increases the amount that you can afford to spend on customer acquisition and increases the ROI of your social marketing strategy.

Why loyal customers drive word of mouth and advocacy

Loyal customers do more than buy your products themselves. They share their love for your product with others, which turns retention into a growth channel. That value shows up in written customer feedback and in everyday word of mouth.

Word of mouth is the most common source of brand discovery among internet users in the United States. And shared social content (the digital version of word of mouth) is the most powerful way to turn brand awareness into consideration.

What drives brand loyalty?

Loyalty isn’t one big gesture. It’s the accumulation of small, repeated signals that a brand is reliable and worth caring about. Researchers

articles.title: Email Marketing in the AI Era: Personalization, Automation & Deliverability
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI adoption in email is concentrated in content production. Personalization, automation, and deliverability, where the bigger revenue gains sit, get far less attention.
  • Personalization is moving from broad segments, like geography and demographics, to individual, predictive targeting.
  • Automation’s share of email revenue grows with company size. Businesses over $51 million in revenue get 71 percent of email revenue from automation versus 11 percent from campaigns.
  • Nearly a fifth of sent emails never reach the inbox, and most of that loss happens before a subscriber has any chance to engage.
  • The programs that win connect personalization, automation, and deliverability into a single system that reinforces itself.

Have you noticed your team is sending more emails than ever, but the results don’t feel any different?

Most marketers are pointing AI at email marketing’s wrong problem. The real opportunity is understanding customer intent, automating decisions, and personalizing experiences at scale. Most teams are using AI to write more emails without fixing the parts of the program that actually drive revenue.

Email personalization, automation, and deliverability are the three areas that actually move that revenue. Inboxes are getting louder as AI makes content creation easier, and louder rarely means more relevant. The rest of this post walks through what’s changing in each area, and how to build them into one connected system.

The AI Shift: What’s Changing in Email Marketing

Marketing teams are under real pressure right now: do more with fewer resources, scale personalization, improve retention and lifetime value, and increase marketing efficiency, all at once. AI looks like the obvious answer.

The problem is where that AI effort is actually going. Ask marketers what their biggest email challenge is today, and list growth tops the list at 29 percent, followed by personalization at 25 percent. Deliverability comes in last, at just 6 percent, even though it’s the foundation everything else depends on. An email that never reaches the inbox can’t be personalized or well-timed enough to matter.

Source

The New Email Marketing Framework

Here’s how the pieces break down:

  1. Personalization: delivering the right message.
  2. Automation: delivering it at the right moment.
  3. Deliverability: making sure it reaches the inbox at all.

You can’t improve these levers in isolation and expect the same lift each time. A gain in one gets erased by a gap in another. Perfect personalization that lands in spam accomplishes nothing, and flawless deliverability paired with generic, one-size-fits-all messaging just means more people ignoring an email they did receive.

Personalization in the AI Era

Most brands are stuck in what amounts to a segmentation trap. They personalize using broad buckets, new versus returning customers, geography, industry, demographics, and call it personalization. Only 34 percent of companies actually use AI-driven or predictive email marketing personalization. Another 24 percent are still at basic audience segmentation, and 5 percent use no personalization at all.

Most teams have the customer data needed for real personalization, they just aren’t using it to predict what happens next. Teams rate themselves strongest in measurement and attribution, with 55 percent calling that capability strong or very advanced. They rate themselves weakest in customer data and identity, at just 37 percent strong or advanced, along with AI skills and governance.

Personalization moves through three stages. Demographic personalization (location, age, gender) is the easiest to set up but produces broad assumptions and low relevance. Behavioral personalization (products viewed, purchases, engagement) produces higher engagement and better conversion. Predictive personalization goes a step further, using purchase likelihood, churn risk, and lifetime value to guide what happens next.

Open rates already vary by age group, from roughly 20.6 percent among 18-24-year-olds up to 25.7 percent among 55-64-year-olds, which makes a strong case for layering behavioral and predictive signals on top of basic demographic segmentation.

articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Engagement rate measures how many people interact with your social content relative to reach, impressions, or follower count. It includes actions like likes, comments, shares, and saves, but not passive views.
  2. The most common formula is engagement rate by reach (ERR): total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. Different formulas suit different goals, from organic posts to paid campaigns.
  3. A good engagement rate typically falls between 1% and 5%, but benchmarks vary significantly by platform and industry. Always compare against your specific platform and industry, not a universal standard.
  4. Tracking engagement rate over time shows which content resonates, which formats to prioritize, and where to adjust your strategy. Perch by Hootsuite automates that tracking across all your accounts, and social media analytics tools can also provide industry benchmarks for comparison.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is a social media metric that measures how much of your audience actively engages with your content. It defines the amount of interaction a piece of content (or a campaign, or a whole account) gets compared to reach or audience size.

Engagement metrics vary by channel, but in general, it’s any action someone takes to interact with your content, including likes, comments, shares, saves, poll responses, messages, or link clicks. Because each platform counts engagement a little differently, it helps to know exactly what actions feed into your social media engagement rate before you calculate it.

Why does engagement rate matter?

Engagement rate matters because it shows whether your content is actually connecting with your audience. When people take the time to like, comment, share, or save a post, it’s a strong signal that they find it interesting or useful.

Second, higher engagement rates help you get better visibility on social media platforms. That’s because social algorithms surface more engaging content to new audiences.

A lot of engagement on your content also makes you look more trustworthy and appealing to first-time profile visitors, especially if there’s an active conversation happening in your comments. For enterprise teams, engagement rate is also one of the clearest ways to prove social ROI to leadership, since it ties content performance to real audience behavior.

What counts as engagement on each platform?

Engagement is any action a user takes to interact with your content, but the specific actions that count vary from platform to platform. Knowing what feeds into the formula helps you calculate an accurate engagement rate and compare performance fairly across channels.

Here’s what typically counts as engagement on each major social network:

  • Instagram: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and replies to Stories.
  • TikTok: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and follows generated by a video.
  • Facebook: Reactions, comments, shares, and clicks on links or buttons.
  • LinkedIn: Reactions, comments, shares (reposts), and clicks.
  • X (Twitter): Likes, replies, reposts, quote posts, and clicks.
  • Pinterest: Saves (repins), comments, clicks, and close-ups.

Passive metrics like impressions and views usually don’t count as engagement on their own, since they measure exposure rather than interaction. When in doubt, check the platform’s analytics to confirm which actions it includes before running your numbers.

How to calculate engagement rate (6 formulas)

The standard engagement rate formula is total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. That said, there are six variations worth knowing, because each one uses a different denominator and answers a slightly different question.

  1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common.
  2. Engagement rate by post (ER post): Best for specific posts.
  3. Engagement rate by impressions (ER impressions): Best for paid content.
  4. Daily engagement rate (Daily ER): Best for long-term analysis.
  5. Engagement rate by views (ER views): Best for video.
  6. Cost per engagement (CPE): Best for influencer marketing or conversion-based campaigns.

1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common

This is the most common engagement rate formula. ERR measures the percentage of people who interact with your content after seeing it.

Here’s how to calculate engagement rate for a single post:

ERR = total number of engagements on a post / reach of that post * 100

To calculate the average ERR across multiple posts, add together the ERR for each post and divide by the total number of posts:

Average ERR = Total ERR / Number of posts

For example: Post 1 (3.4%) + Post 2 (3.5%) / 2 = 3.45%

Pros: Because not all followers see every post, ERR is often more accurate than follower-based metrics, especially in algorithm-driven feeds. Reach includes both followers and non-followers who discover content through search, shares, hashtags, and recommendations.

Cons: Reach can fluctuate for a variety of reasons, making it a difficult variable to control. ...
